title: Two days selling olives at a food expo

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Two days, one olive kiosk, and roughly three hundred dollars in sales. Was it worth it?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Three hundred dollars doesn't sound like a lot. Why bother?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Antoine admits the number is small. He went to Expo Manger Santé 2023 in Montreal to see both sides: the vendor view at the kiosk, and the visitor view, meaning what he'd actually reorder.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: So what worked at the kiosk?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Short tastings with a story, like the origin and the brine. Honest recommendations like 'try this one if you like such-and-such.' And repeat visitors on day two. What didn't work: competing with loud neighbors on price, and selling in bulk without bags ready.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Small sample cups, because people commit when it's one bite. Price cards at eye level, so nobody has to ask twice. And restock your best seller for day two, since people come back for what they tasted the day before.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: What about the food on the other side of the aisle?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: He liked Gen V lettuces, crisp enough to notice after a day of crackers and dips. The neighbors at Mate Libre were the best part of the row, and he calls their matéina line the find he texted friends about. He also plans to add Wise smoothie mixes to his rushed mornings.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Hall photos are by OS7Media, with permission. His own booth shots are his.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Yes, with better kiosk inventory planning and more water bottles. The full write-up has the tables and the booth photos.
